content: The certainty of evidence regarding the use of vaginal misoprostol compared to sublingual misoprostol is moderate. Women in the vaginal misoprostol group reported higher satisfaction compared to those in the sublingual group, but the certainty of this evidence is very low. Pre-procedure cervical dilation was lower in the vaginal misoprostol group compared to the sublingual group, with very low certainty of evidence. More women in the vaginal misoprostol group required additional dilation compared to the sublingual group, with low certainty of evidence. The time to complete the procedure was longer with vaginal misoprostol compared to sublingual misoprostol, with moderate certainty of evidence. Overall, the comparison favors sublingual misoprostol. When comparing sublingual misoprostol to oral misoprostol, pre-procedure cervical dilation was greater in the sublingual group, with moderate certainty of evidence. Fewer women in the sublingual group required further dilation compared to the oral group, with low certainty of evidence. No undesirable effects were noted, and the intervention favors sublingual misoprostol. In a sub-analysis of interval timing, a 3-hour interval (400 μg vaginal) resulted in greater pre-procedure cervical dilation compared to a 2-hour interval (600 μg vaginal), with high certainty of evidence. Fewer women in the 3-hour interval group required further dilation and experienced pain during cervical priming compared to the 2-hour interval group, with high certainty of evidence. No undesirable effects were noted, and the intervention may favor the 3-hour interval. When comparing a 3-hour interval to a 1-hour interval, pre-procedure cervical dilation was greater in the 3-hour interval group (vaginal and sublingual) compared to the 1-hour interval group, with moderate certainty of evidence. Fewer women in the 3-hour interval group experienced nausea compared to the 1-hour interval group, with low certainty of evidence. However, pre-procedure cervical dilation was lower in the 3-hour sublingual group compared to the 1-hour sublingual group, with moderate certainty of evidence. More women in the 3-hour interval group experienced pain during cervical priming compared to the 1-hour interval group, with low to moderate certainty of evidence. The time to complete the procedure was longer in the 3-hour interval group compared to the 1-hour interval group, with moderate certainty of evidence. The intervention may favor the 3-hour interval. In a sub-analysis of misoprostol dosage, 400 μg (oral, vaginal, sublingual) resulted in greater pre-procedure cervical dilation compared to 200 μg, with high certainty of evidence for oral administration, moderate for sublingual, and low for vaginal. Fewer women in the 400 μg group (vaginal, sublingual) required further dilation compared to the 200 μg group, with moderate certainty of evidence for sublingual and high for vaginal. The time to complete the procedure was shorter with 400 μg (vaginal, sublingual) compared to 200 μg, with moderate certainty of evidence. More women in the 400 μg group experienced pain during cervical priming compared to the 200 μg group, with low to high certainty of evidence. The intervention favors 400 μg misoprostol. When comparing misoprostol to mifepristone, the time to complete the procedure was shorter with misoprostol, with moderate certainty of evidence. Fewer women in the misoprostol group experienced cramping and vomiting compared to the mifepristone group, with very low certainty of evidence. Pre-procedure cervical dilation was lower in the misoprostol group compared to the mifepristone group, with moderate certainty of evidence. More women in the misoprostol group experienced nausea compared to the mifepristone group, with very low certainty of evidence. The balance of effects may favor the comparison. When comparing misoprostol to a combination of mifepristone and misoprostol, fewer women in the misoprostol group experienced abdominal pain/cramping compared to the combination group, with very low certainty of evidence. There was no difference in nausea between the two groups, with very low certainty of evidence. Pre-procedure cervical dilation was lower in the misoprostol group compared to the combination group, with moderate certainty of evidence. The time to complete the procedure was longer with misoprostol compared to the combination, with moderate certainty of evidence. More women in the misoprostol group experienced vomiting compared to the combination group, with very low certainty of evidence. The balance of effects favors the comparison. When comparing mifepristone to placebo, pre-procedure cervical dilation was greater in the mifepristone group, with high certainty of evidence. Fewer women in the mifepristone group required further dilation compared to the placebo group, with low certainty of evidence. No undesirable effects were noted, and the intervention favors mifepristone. When comparing mifepristone to a combination of mifepristone and misoprostol, there was no difference in nausea between the two groups, with low certainty of evidence. Pre-procedure cervical dilation was lower in the mifepristone group compared to the combination group, with moderate certainty of evidence. The time to complete the procedure was longer with mifepristone compared to the combination, with moderate certainty of evidence. More women in the mifepristone group experienced vomiting and abdominal cramping compared to the combination group, with very low certainty of evidence. The balance of effects favors the comparison. When comparing osmotic dilators to placebo, mean cervical dilation was higher in the osmotic dilator group. No meta-analysis or GRADE assessment was performed. When comparing misoprostol to laminaria, fewer women in the misoprostol group (400 μg) required further dilation compared to the laminaria group, with moderate certainty of evidence. More women in the misoprostol group expressed greater satisfaction with their cervical ripening method compared to the laminaria group, with moderate certainty of evidence. However, more women in the misoprostol group required further dilation compared to the laminaria group, with low certainty of evidence. The intervention may favor misoprostol. When comparing misoprostol to Dilapan, the time to complete the procedure was shorter with misoprostol, with high certainty of evidence. Fewer women in the misoprostol group required re-aspiration compared to the Dilapan group, with low certainty of evidence. There was no difference in cervical laceration/injury between the two groups, with low certainty of evidence. Pre-procedure cervical dilation was lower in the misoprostol group compared to the Dilapan group, with high certainty of evidence. More women in the misoprostol group required further dilation compared to the Dilapan group, with low certainty of evidence. The balance of effects shows no difference between the intervention and comparison. Additional considerations include uncertainty about the variability in how people value the main outcomes, moderate costs associated with the intervention, and the potential for reduced health equity. The intervention's acceptability to key stakeholders and feasibility of implementation remain uncertain.
